newsitem.title: UK: New dinosaur species discovered in England.
newsitem.headline: New dinosaur species discovered in England.

text.p: Remains of a frightening, flesh-eating dinosaur found on England's southern coast are from a new species, British scientists said on Thursday. The 26-foot-long (eight-metre long) Neovenator probably fed on herds of plant-eating Iguanadons, which were common in the area, Steve Hutt of the Museum of Isle of Wight Geology said.
The dinosaur, scientifically named Neovenator Salerii after the Salero family on whose land the fossils were found, lived 120 million years ago.

Neovenator was certainly the major flesh-eater around in the UK at this time," Hutt told the Times newspaper. Experts have confirmed that Neovenator is a previously unknown species, distantly related to the Allosaurus from North America but lighter and quicker. "It is like comparing a tiger to a cheetah, I suppose," Hutt said.
It probably ran down its prey like a cheetah and used its long claws and teeth to tear it apart, Hutt said.
The fossilised bones were first found in 1978 but scientists had only recently dug them all out. Hutt was delighted to find such a complete skeleton.
"It's great, especially when we are chipping the mud off these beautiful black bones and you realise that you have something new to science," he told ITN television.
Millions of years ago the Isle of Wight, now just off England's south coast in the chilly Channel, was a warm, subtropical region.
"Reptiles thrive in warm climates -- they get bigger and bigger," Hutt told ITN.
The Isle of Wight is a rich source of dinosaur fossils, both because so many lived there and because its high cliffs are falling off into the sea.
"The only good thing about coastal erosion is that it reveals these fossils," Hutt said.
